quickRef.title: Right-triangle height
quickRef.intro: Take a right triangle and drop a line from the right-angle corner $C$ **straight down** to the long side $AB$ (the hypotenuse). That line is the height $h$. It cuts the long side into two pieces, $p$ and $q$, so the whole long side is $c=p+q$. It also splits the triangle into two smaller triangles with the **same shape** as the big one, which is why these four shortcuts work. Check them on a 3-4-5 triangle: $p=1.8$, $q=3.2$, $h=2.4$.

quickRef.title: Symmetry
quickRef.intro: A graph is symmetric about a line when folding along that line makes the two halves match. Each rule below is a swap: apply it to the equation, and if the equation comes back unchanged, the graph has that symmetry. The point mapping says where each point lands.

items.name: Across $x=a$
items.note: same as $f(2a-x)=f(x)$; $(x,y)\to(2a-x,y)$. $f(2+d)=f(2-d)$ means symmetric about $x=2$

items.name: Across the $x$-axis
items.note: $y\to-y$ leaves the equation unchanged, e.g. $x=y^2$; never a function unless it is $y=0$

items.name: Across $y=b$
items.note: $y\to2b-y$ leaves it unchanged: $b+d$ and $b-d$ average to $b$

items.name: Across $y=x$
items.note: swap $x$ and $y$; a function symmetric here is its own inverse, $f(f(x))=x$

items.name: Across $y=-x$
items.note: swap, then make both negative

items.name: Across $y=x+c$
items.note: $c=0$ gives the $y=x$ rule

items.name: Reflect $y=f(x)$
items.note: this moves the graph; the rules above only test it. For $f^{-1}$, swap $x$ and $y$, then solve for $y$

items.name: Line up $n$ things
items.note: $4! = 4\times3\times2\times1 = 24$

items.name: Choose $k$ of $n$
items.note: order doesn't matter

items.name: With repeats
items.note: AABB has $\frac{4!}{2!\,2!}=6$ orders

items.name: A block of $k$ glued people
items.note: tape the $k$ people into one block. **Items** = the new total count after grouping: if you start with $n$ people, the $k$ in the tape become 1, so items $=n-k+1$ (the block plus everyone else). Line up the items, then multiply by $k!$ for the orders inside the block. 6 people with R and S together: $5!\times2!=240$. If A must sit between B and C, the block has only 2 orders (BAC, CAB), so $\times2!$, not $\times3!$

items.name: Together + a banned seat
items.note: 6 people in a row, R next to S, T not at either end. Tape R and S together: 5 items. T takes one of the 3 middle spots, the other 4 items fill the rest, and R, S can swap. Do the tape first, then the picky person

items.name: $n$ identical things into $k$ groups
items.note: stars and bars. Share 5 identical candies among 3 kids: draw the candies as 5 stars and add $k-1=2$ bars to cut them into 3 groups. Each row of 5 stars and 2 bars is one way to share, so count the rows: 7 spots, pick the 2 for the bars, $\tbinom72=21$. Zero is allowed (a bar at an end, or two bars side by side). If everyone needs **at least 1**, hand out 1 each first, then share the rest: $\tbinom{n-1}{k-1}=\tbinom42=6$. The things must be identical but the groups different (kids, boxes)

items.name: At least one
items.note: listing every way it happens once, twice, ... is long; instead find the chance it never happens and take that away from 1. Three coin flips: $P(\text{at least one head}) = 1-(\tfrac12)^3=\tfrac78$

items.name: Two groups
items.note: this = the total. $A$ + $B$ counts the middle (both) **twice**, so take it away once, then add the people in neither circle. 30 take French, 25 Spanish, 10 both, 5 neither: total $=30+25-10+5=50$. Turned around, both $=A+B+\text{neither}-\text{total}$. Watch the words: "$A$" means everyone in $A$, including those also in $B$; "only $A$" means $A-\text{both}$

items.name: Number of factors
items.note: for $n = 2^a\times3^b$ (any primes); counts 1 and $n$

items.name: Last digits repeat
items.note: units digit of powers; 4 and 9 every 2; 0, 1, 5, 6 never change

items.name: If $x+\frac1x=s$
items.note: square both sides

items.name: Inequality rule
items.note: when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, turn the sign around: $<$ becomes $>$. From $-2x<6$, divide by $-2$: $x>-3$. Adding or subtracting never flips it

items.name: Arithmetic: $n$-th term
items.note: $d$ = the fixed gap between terms. $3, 7, 11, \dots$: $a_{10}=3+9\times4=39$

items.name: Arithmetic: sum
items.note: number of terms × the average of the first and last. $1+2+\cdots+100=100\times\tfrac{101}{2}=5050$

items.name: Arithmetic: how many terms
items.note: the $+1$ counts the first term. Multiples of 3 from 12 to 99: $\tfrac{99-12}{3}+1=30$

items.name: Geometric: $n$-th term
items.note: $r$ = the fixed ratio between terms. $3, 6, 12, \dots$: $a_6=3\times2^5=96$

items.name: Geometric: sum forever
items.note: only when $-1<r<1$, so the terms shrink to 0. $8+4+2+1+\cdots=\tfrac{8}{1-\frac12}=16$

items.name: Simple interest
items.note: the same $Pr$ is added every year; $r$ as a decimal, $t$ in years. 1000 at 5% for 3 years: $1000\times1.15=1150$

items.name: Compound interest
items.note: $n$ = times a year it is added (yearly 1, twice a year 2, quarterly 4, monthly 12). 1000 at 10% yearly for 2 years: $1000\times1.1^2=1210$, vs 1200 simple

items.name: Percent change
items.note: divide by where you started

items.name: Up $p$%
items.note: up 700% means ×8, not ×7

items.name: Average of two groups
items.note: big groups count more

items.name: Bell curve
items.note: SD = standard deviation

items.name: Above +1 SD
items.note: on a bell curve; same share below $-1$ SD

items.name: Above +2 SD
items.note: on a bell curve; same share below $-2$ SD

items.name: Median position
items.note: a .5 position: average the two values around it

items.name: Q1 position
items.note: same as the median of the lower half; an odd count leaves the median out

items.name: Q3 position
items.note: the mirror of Q1: 10 numbers give $x_3$ and $x_8$

items.tex: \footnotesize\begin{gathered}Q_1=\text{median of lower half}\\ Q_3=\text{median of upper half}\end{gathered}

quickRef.title: Density curves
quickRef.intro: A density curve shows how likely each value of $X$ is. The **area** under it between two numbers is the chance $X$ lands between them. Each card below is one shortcut for finding that area.

items.name: Total area
items.note: The chance $X$ lands between $a$ and $b$ is the **area** above that stretch, never the height of the curve. All of it together is 100%, so the whole area is 1.

formats.title: Quantitative Comparison
rules: Your job is to try to **break** it. Try two very different numbers. If the winner changes, the answer is (D).
Good numbers to try: $0$, $1$, $-1$, $\frac12$, a big number, and both ends of any allowed range.
No letters, just numbers? Then it can't be (D). Just work it out.
Picture 'not drawn to scale' shapes stretched or squished in every way the facts allow.

formats.title: Multiple choice, one answer
rules: Look at the answers first. They tell you how exact you need to be.
Stuck setting it up? Try the middle answer in the question and see if it's too big or too small.
No numbers given? Make some up (like 100 for percents).
The wrong answers are built from common mistakes, so finding your number among the choices doesn't prove it's right.

formats.title: Select all that apply
rules: All or nothing: no partial credit. Judge each choice yes/no on its own.
First find the rule (a range, 'multiples of 47', 'odd numbers from 5 to 65'), then test every choice against it, including **both ends**.
Picking every choice is almost never right. Look for the one built to fail.

formats.title: Numeric Entry
rules: There are no choices to catch a mistake, so reread the last sentence and **underline what they're asking for**.
Plug your answer back into the question to check it.
Fractions don't need simplifying. Negative answers are allowed.

formats.title: Charts & tables
rules: Read the title, labels and units before you start.
Estimate first. The answers are often far apart.
For 'percent of' and 'percent more than', check what you're dividing by.

pacing: About **1:45 per question**: 12 questions in 21 minutes, then 15 in 26.
If you're at **2:30** with no plan, guess, mark it, and move on. You can come back.
Do the easy ones first; come back to marked ones with the time you saved.
Practice with the timer on (exam mode), so your score is real.
A 170 means 0–2 mistakes. The easiest points to win back are comparison traps and misreading the question.

cards.text: Almost every circle problem is a **right triangle** in disguise. Draw a line from the center to a point on the circle: that's the radius, and it's usually the long side of a right triangle.

cards.q: A square has all four corners on a circle of radius 5. What is the area of the square?
steps: The square's diagonal (corner to corner) goes straight across the circle, so the diagonal is $2\times5=10$.
A square with diagonal $d$ has area $\frac{d^2}{2}$.
Area $=\frac{100}{2}=50$. (Quick check with the shortcut: $2r^2=2\times25=50$.)

cards.text: Learn two special triangles by heart. Most hard triangle questions are one of them in disguise; you just have to **cut the shape** the right way.

cards.q: In triangle $ABC$, angle $B=30^\circ$ and side $BC=8$. How long is the height from $C$ straight down to side $AB$?
steps: Drop the height from $C$. On the $B$ side you get a 30-60-90 triangle, and $BC=8$ is its longest side.
In a 30-60-90 triangle, the side across from $30^\circ$ is **half** the longest side.
The height is across from the $30^\circ$ angle, so it is $\frac82=4$.

cards.text: Slope just means 'how far **up** for each step **right**'. Most line questions come down to slope.

cards.q: A line goes through $(1, 6)$ and is perpendicular to a line with slope $\frac23$. Where does it cross the $x$-axis?
steps: Perpendicular slope: flip the fraction and change the sign. $\frac23\to-\frac32$.
$-\frac32$ means every 2 steps right, the line drops 3.
To get from $y=6$ down to $y=0$ it drops 6. That takes $2\times2=4$ steps right.
$x=1+4=5$, so it crosses at $(5, 0)$.

cards.text: $x$-intercept: set $y=0$ · $y$-intercept: set $x=0$

cards.text: a square also needs **equal** adjacent sides

cards.name: Point-to-line formula
cards.text: move everything to one side first
Walk all the way around any shape and you turn one full circle, so the outside angles **always add up to $360^\circ$**. That one fact solves most polygon angle questions.

cards.q: Each inside angle of a regular polygon is $140^\circ$. How many diagonals does it have?
steps: Inside + outside angle make a straight line, so the outside angle is $180-140=40^\circ$.
All outside angles add to $360^\circ$, so it has $\frac{360}{40}=9$ sides.
Diagonals $=\frac{9\times(9-3)}{2}=\frac{54}{2}=27$.

cards.name: "Which could be" a length

cards.note: a triangle's third side: $|a-b|<c<a+b$

cards.name: Longest stick in a box
cards.note: corner to opposite corner; a cube: $s\sqrt3$

cards.text: drop two heights: overhang $=\frac{b_2-b_1}{2}$ each side
cards.note: then Pythagoras; 3-4-5 / 6-8-10 are common

cards.name: Lengths can be fractions
cards.text: sides aren't whole numbers unless the question says so
cards.note: a "could be" answer like $2.5$ is still allowed

cards.name: Asked for diagonals
cards.text: finding $n$ is only the middle step

patterns.title: Together + a banned seat: glue first, then the picky one
patterns.idea: When a problem has a **must sit together** rule and a **seat ban**, work in this order. (1) **Glue** the together people into one item and write $\times k!$ for their inside orders straight away. (2) **Seat the picky item.** (3) Fill the rest in $m!$ ways. Order matters because a single person seated first is a **wall**: it splits the empty seats into a left part and a right part, and a pair then needs casework to find two seats side by side. After gluing, every item takes one seat, so there is nothing left to split.

patterns.title: Stars and bars: identical things into groups
patterns.idea: To share $n$ **identical** things among $k$ groups (a group may get none), picture $n$ stars in a row and $k-1$ dividers placed among them. Each arrangement is one way to share, so there are $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$ ways. The cases below are this same method in different disguises.

cards.text: Counting is **filling slots**. Count the choices for each slot and multiply, and always fill the **pickiest** slot first.

cards.q: In how many ways can 5 people stand in a line if Sam and Tia must stand next to each other?
steps: Tape Sam and Tia together into one block. Now you're lining up 4 things: $4!=24$ ways.
Inside the block they can be Sam-Tia or Tia-Sam: $\times2$.
$24\times2=48$ ways.

cards.name: Must NOT be together
cards.text: all ways − ways together

cards.name: Pickiest first
cards.text: seat the person with rules before anyone else
cards.example: Ann not at either end of 8 seats: $6\times7!$

cards.name: Choices that limit each other
cards.text: fill the most limited spot first, or split into cases
cards.example: odd 3-digit numbers, no repeats: units $5$, hundreds $8$, tens $8$: $320$

cards.name: "Digits in decreasing order"
cards.text: the order is fixed: just **choose** the digits, $\binom nk$

cards.name: Check a counting method
cards.text: run it on a tiny version and list every case by hand
cards.example: 4 people at a round table: $(4-1)!=6$, list them to confirm

cards.name: Order of a few named people
cards.text: every order equally likely
cards.note: A ahead of B: $\frac12$; one order of 3 named people: $\frac16$

cards.name: Every pair once
cards.note: handshakes, round-robin games, lines through $n$ points

cards.name: The $k$th draw, nothing known before it
cards.text: same chance as the **first** draw
cards.note: without replacement, earlier draws unseen

cards.name: Multiply only independent steps
cards.text: if one step changes the next step's options, count it that way
cards.example: 2-letter code from A–E, no repeats: $5\times4=20$, not $5^2$

cards.name: None of A, B or C
cards.note: subtracting the pair overlaps removes the all-three group once too often: add it back

cards.name: Banned seat + glued pair
cards.text: glue **first**, then seat the picky one
cards.note: seating them first splits the row and forces casework

cards.name: Round table
cards.note: fix one seat first, then glue as usual

cards.name: Repeated people
cards.text: glue, then divide by the repeats
cards.note: e.g. two identical flags

cards.name: Different items
cards.note: each item picks a group

cards.name: Unordered factorizations
cards.text: list them by hand
cards.note: "sets of 3 integers whose product is 72"

cards.name: Product of digits
cards.text: list digit sets, then $\frac{4!}{\text{repeats}!}$ each
cards.note: "4-digit numbers whose digits multiply to 24"

cards.name: Glue, then the picky one
cards.q: Six people (R, S, T, A, B, C) sit in a row of 6 seats. R and S must sit next to each other, and T may not sit in either end seat. How many seatings are possible?
cards.spot: 'next to each other' or 'together', plus a person banned from some seats.

steps: **Glue:** tape R and S into one item, [RS], and write $\times2!$ now (RS or SR). That leaves 5 items for 5 merged seats.
**Picky one:** the end items of the 5 merged seats still sit in the real end seats, so T takes seat 2, 3 or 4: $3$ ways.
**Everyone else:** [RS], A, B and C fill the 4 open seats: $4!=24$.
$3\times4!\times2!=3\times24\times2=\mathbf{144}$.

cards.name: The trap: seating T before gluing
cards.q: Same problem, but T is seated first in the 6 single seats. Where does that go wrong?
cards.spot: you seated one person, then went looking for two seats side by side.

steps: T has 4 seats (2 to 5), and wherever it sits it splits the empty seats. T in seat 2 leaves [1] and [3, 4, 5, 6]. T in seat 3 leaves [1, 2] and [4, 5, 6].
Either way R and S have exactly **3** side-by-side pairs, so there are $4\times3=12$ ways to pick T's seat and the pair. (Seats 4 and 5 mirror seats 3 and 2.)
**The slip:** $\frac{3!}{2!}=3$ only picks *which* pair. R and S can sit in it 2 ways, so multiply by $2!$.
A, B and C take the last 3 seats in $3!=6$ ways: $12\times2\times6=\mathbf{144}$. Drop the $\times2$ and you get $72$, a likely wrong choice. Gluing first skips all of this casework.

cards.name: A trio with a fixed middle
cards.q: Six people sit in a row, and T must sit directly between R and S. How many seatings are possible?
cards.spot: 'between', 'flanked by', 'with one on each side'.
steps: Glue [R T S] into one item. T is pinned to the middle, so only the ends swap: $\times2!$, not $\times3!$.
That leaves 4 items (the trio, A, B, C): $4!=24$.
$24\times2=\mathbf{48}$.

cards.name: Apart instead of together: subtract
cards.q: Six people sit in a row. R and S may **not** sit next to each other, and T may not sit in either end seat. How many seatings are possible?
cards.spot: 'not next to each other', together with a second rule.
steps: Count with T's rule only: T has 4 seats and the other 5 people fill the rest, $4\times5!=480$.
Subtract the seatings where R and S **are** together, with T's rule kept: $144$ (case 1).
$480-144=\mathbf{336}$. Keep every other rule in both counts, or the subtraction is wrong.

cards.name: The banned person is inside the block
cards.q: Six people sit in a row. R and S must sit next to each other, and R may not sit in either end seat. How many seatings are possible?
cards.spot: the person with the seat ban is one of the glued people.
steps: You can't just keep the block off the ends: [SR] in seats 1 and 2 is fine, since R is not on the end. The flip and the seat interact, so count all and subtract.
All seatings with R and S together: $5!\times2!=240$.
Bad ones: R in seat 1 forces S into seat 2, and the other 4 fill in $4!=24$ ways. R in seat 6 gives another $24$.

cards.name: Identical items to people, zero allowed
cards.q: In how many ways can 10 identical cookies go to 4 children if a child may get none?
cards.spot: 'identical' or 'indistinguishable' items, and 'may receive none'.
steps: $n=10$ cookies (stars), $k=4$ children (groups).

cards.name: At least one each
cards.q: Same 10 cookies and 4 children, but each child gets at least one.
cards.spot: 'at least one', 'no group is empty', 'positive integers'.
steps: Hand 1 cookie to each child first: $10-4=6$ left.

cards.name: Different minimums
cards.q: How many integer solutions does $x+y+z=15$ have with $x\ge2$, $y\ge3$, $z\ge0$?
cards.spot: an equation adding up to a total, with $\ge$ limits under it.
steps: Pay the minimums first: $15-2-3-0=10$ left.

cards.name: Menu or store choice (repeats allowed)
cards.q: A shop sells 4 kinds of flower. How many different bouquets of 7 flowers can you make?
cards.spot: picking $n$ things from $k$ kinds, order doesn't matter, repeats allowed.
steps: The kinds are the groups ($k=4$); the picks are the stars ($n=7$).

cards.name: Digit sum of 9 or less
cards.q: How many 4-digit positive integers have digits that add up to 7?
cards.spot: 'sum of the digits' with a target of 9 or less, so no digit can go over 9.
steps: Put 1 in the thousands place so it can't be 0: $7-1=6$ left.
Now $n=6$, $k=4$ digit slots: $\binom{9}{3}=\mathbf{84}$.

cards.name: Ordered factorization
cards.q: How many ordered triples $(a,b,c)$ of positive integers have $abc=72$?
cards.spot: 'ordered' triples (or pairs, quadruples) multiplying to a number.
steps: $72=2^3\times3^2$. Each prime's copies are identical stars; $a$, $b$, $c$ are the 3 groups.
Three 2s into 3 groups: $\binom{5}{2}=10$. Two 3s into 3 groups: $\binom{4}{2}=6$.
Multiply: $10\times6=\mathbf{60}$.

cards.name: Digit sum just over 9: subtract the overflows
cards.q: How many 3-digit numbers have digits that add up to 11?
cards.spot: a digit sum of 10 or more, so one digit could wrongly reach 10.
steps: Give the hundreds digit 1 first (it can't be 0). That leaves 10 to share over 3 digits: $\binom{12}{2}=66$ ways.
Some of those give one digit 10 or more, which isn't a digit. Take them out.
Hundreds too big: it already has 1, so give it 9 more, leaving 1: $\binom{3}{2}=3$ bad ways. Tens too big: give it 10, leaving 0: $1$ bad way. Ones: also $1$.

cards.name: Digit sum near the max: count down from 999
cards.q: How many 3-digit numbers have digits that add up to 24?
cards.spot: a digit sum close to the largest possible ($27$ for 3 digits).
steps: Start at 999 (digit sum 27) and take away $27-24=3$ in total, spread over the digits.
Taking away only 3 can't push any digit below 0 or turn the first digit into 0, so nothing needs to be ruled out.
Share 3 'take-aways' among 3 digits: $\binom{5}{2}=\mathbf{10}$.

cards.text: When people are in two groups, the ones in **both** get counted twice. Every group formula is just fixing that double count.

cards.q: Of 40 students, 25 play soccer and 22 play basketball. What is the fewest number who could play both?
steps: $25+22=47$, but there are only 40 students.
So at least $47-40=7$ students were counted twice.
The fewest who play both is **7** (that's when every student plays at least one).

cards.name: Three groups, "exactly two" known
cards.note: with the pair overlaps instead: $A+B+C-(AB+AC+BC)+ABC+\text{neither}$

cards.name: Max or min of "only A" or "neither"
cards.text: push "both" to its smallest or biggest value first

cards.name: Two yes/no traits
cards.text: 2×2 table with totals: rows and columns add up, so missing cells fall out
cards.example: 60 people, 25 men, 40 voters, 10 men vote: women non-voters $35-30=5$

cards.name: Make one thing as big as possible
cards.text: make everything else as **small** as allowed
cards.example: 5 different positive integers, average 10: biggest is $50-(1+2+3+4)=40$

cards.name: Fewest picks to guarantee $k$ alike
cards.note: $n$ kinds: plan the worst luck, then add 1; a kind with fewer than $k-1$ items gives only what it has

cards.name: Overlap forced by the total
cards.text: if $A+B>$ total, at least $A+B-$total are in **both**
cards.note: you can't assume the groups don't overlap
cards.example: 30 like tea, 25 coffee, 40 people: at least $15$ like both

cards.name: "Neither" isn't always 0
cards.text: unless everyone is said to be in a group, leave room for neither
cards.note: neither $>0$ raises the smallest possible "both"

cards.name: "Could be" an overlap
cards.text: the value must sit between the smallest and largest "both"
cards.example: both ranges $15$–$25$: $12$ is impossible, whatever its parity

patterns.title: "Must be" questions: test at least two numbers
patterns.idea: When a question has a letter and asks what **must** be true (or a QC asks which is bigger), it's asking about **every** number allowed. One number can only rule a choice out. It can't prove one. So always test **two**, and make the second one **different in kind** from the first: the next multiple, the other parity, a negative, a fraction, a long thin shape, a lopsided list. If a choice passes both tests, find the reason it always works before you pick it.

patterns.title: Far-off terms: find the cycle, or cancel
patterns.idea: Asked for the 50th term, the 100th digit or a sum of 99 terms? Look at the formula first. If each term is built **only from the term before it** (no $k$ anywhere), the values must loop: write terms until one repeats, then jump ahead with the remainder. If **$k$ itself sits in a denominator**, the terms never loop; split each one into two fractions and watch the middle of the sum cancel.

cards.text: Remainders and last digits **repeat in a pattern**. Find the pattern with the first few powers, and you never have to work out a huge number.

cards.q: What is the last digit of $7^{43}$?
steps: Last digits of $7^1, 7^2, 7^3, 7^4$: 7, 9, 3, 1. Then it starts over, so the pattern repeats every 4.
$43=40+3$. The 40 is ten full rounds, so we land on the **3rd** spot.
The 3rd spot is **3**.

cards.name: Remainder of a big product or power
cards.text: swap any number for its remainder first

cards.name: Units-digit cycles
cards.text: each base repeats at its **own** speed

cards.name: Odd number of factors
cards.text: only perfect squares
cards.note: factors pair up as $d$ and $\frac nd$, except $\sqrt n$

cards.name: Far-off remainder
cards.text: write the first few until they repeat, then jump by the cycle

cards.name: "Remainder 5 when divided by 6"
cards.note: the smallest is $5$ itself ($q=0$), easy to forget

cards.name: Comparing numbers of factors
cards.text: test $1$, a prime, a prime power **and** a mix like $30$
cards.note: they differ: $1$ has 1, a prime 2, $p^2$ 3, $30$ has 8

cards.name: Power of $p$ in $n!$
cards.note: trailing zeros of $n!$: count the 5s

cards.name: Same remainder $r$ for several divisors
cards.note: each the same amount **short**: LCM·$k$ minus that amount
cards.example: rem 2 by 3, 4, 5: $60k+2$; rem 2 by 3 and 3 by 4: $12k-1$

cards.name: Adding powers
cards.text: pull out the smallest power
cards.note: $2^3+2^4\ne2^7$; equal powers stack: $2^n+2^n=2^{n+1}$

cards.name: Two bases, two cycles
cards.text: find each base's cycle, then repeat every LCM

cards.name: Testing only primes
cards.text: also try $1$, a prime power ($4$, $8$) and a composite ($6$, $12$)
cards.note: every prime has exactly 2 factors, so primes hide the differences

cards.name: "Could be" / "possible value"
cards.text: one number that works proves it: stop

cards.name: Only numbers in the question
cards.text: nothing can vary: just calculate

cards.name: A choice passed two test numbers
cards.text: that's not proof it **must** hold
cards.note: find the reason, or try a very different third number

cards.name: Remainder 0
cards.text: the **last** spot of the cycle

cards.name: Gaps of 2
cards.note: keep the $\frac12$; **two** pieces survive at each end

cards.name: "Must be a divisor"
cards.q: $n$ is a positive multiple of 3. Which of these must divide $n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)$? $9$, $15$, $40$, $72$, $120$, $180$. Indicate all.
cards.spot: "must be a divisor / factor / multiple of", where the letter only has to fit a rule.
steps: First test, $n=3$: $3\cdot4\cdot5\cdot6=360$. All six divide it. Stopping here gets the question wrong.
Second test, $n=6$: $6\cdot7\cdot8\cdot9=3024$. Only $9$ and $72$ divide it, so $15$, $40$, $120$ and $180$ are out.

The reason: four numbers in a row always include two evens, and one of those is a multiple of 4, so there's an $8$. Both $n$ and $n+3$ are multiples of 3, so there's a $9$. That makes $8\times9=72$ every time. Answer: $\mathbf{9}$ **and** $\mathbf{72}$.
It's the same trap when $n$ is a multiple of 5: $n=5$ gives $1680$, which passes $16$, $24$, $35$, $48$, $120$ and $240$. $n=10$ gives $17160$, which leaves only $24$ and $120$.

cards.name: The obvious number is too nice
cards.q: $n$ is a positive integer and $n^2$ is a multiple of 12. Which must divide $n$? $4$, $6$, $12$, $36$.
cards.spot: your first pick is the number in the question (12) or a round number that has extra factors.
steps: $n=12$ works ($144$ is a multiple of 12) and passes $4$, $6$ and $12$.
Now try the **smallest** $n$ that fits: $n=6$, since $36$ is a multiple of 12. Only $6$ divides it.
The reason: $n^2$ needs $2^2\cdot3$, so $n$ needs only one 2 and one 3. Answer: $\mathbf{6}$ only.

cards.name: "Must be true" about a sign or size
cards.q: $x^2>x$. Which must be true? I. $x>1$  II. $x^3>x^2$  III. $x\ne0$
cards.spot: an inequality where a negative or a fraction behaves differently from a positive whole number.
steps: $x=2$: all three are true.
$x=-1$: $1>-1$, so it fits. But I is false, and II is false ($-1>1$ is false).
III: $x=0$ gives $0>0$, which is false, so $x$ is never 0. Answer: **III only**.
Good second numbers: $-1$, $\frac12$, $-\frac12$, $0$ (if it's allowed), and a big number.

cards.name: Remainders
cards.q: $n$ leaves a remainder of 4 when divided by 6. Quantity A: the remainder when $n$ is divided by 4. Quantity B: $1$.
cards.spot: a remainder rule for one number, but the question divides by a different number.
steps: List the numbers that fit: $4, 10, 16, 22, \dots$
$n=4$: remainder $0$, so B is bigger. $n=10$: remainder $2$, so A is bigger.
The winner changes, so the answer is **(D)**. If the first two agree, try the third number on the list too. Remainders often repeat in a cycle of 2 or 3.

cards.name: Shapes with one fixed measure
cards.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 20. Quantity A: its area. Quantity B: $20$.
cards.spot: a shape where only the perimeter, area or one side is fixed (or "not drawn to scale").
steps: A square, $5\times5$: area $25$, so A is bigger.
A long thin one, $9\times1$: area $9$, so B is bigger. The answer is **(D)**.
Always try the most even shape (a square, an equilateral triangle) **and** the most stretched one.

cards.name: A list you're not given
cards.q: Five different positive integers have a mean of 10. Quantity A: their median. Quantity B: $10$.
cards.spot: only the mean, count or range is given. The numbers themselves are left to you.
steps: Evenly spaced, $8,9,10,11,12$: median $10$, so they're equal.
Pushed low, $1,2,3,4,40$: median $3$, so B is bigger. The answer is **(D)**.
Try an evenly spaced list **and** a lopsided one (one huge value, or a bunch of tied values).

cards.name: Term built only from the one before
cards.q: $t_1=2$ and $t_{k+1}=\frac{t_k-1}{t_k+1}$ for $k\ge1$. What is $t_{50}$?
cards.spot: the rule uses $t_k$ but never $k$ itself, often inside a fraction.
steps: Write terms: $t_1=2$, $t_2=\frac13$, $t_3=-\frac12$, $t_4=-3$, $t_5=2$. Back to the start, so the cycle is 4 long.
$50=(4\times12)+\mathbf{2}$. Twelve full loops, then 2 more steps.
Remainder 2 means the 2nd spot: $t_{50}=t_2=\mathbf{\tfrac13}$.

cards.name: Sum that skips terms
cards.q: Same sequence. What is $t_3+t_6+t_9+\cdots+t_{60}$?
cards.spot: only every 2nd, 3rd... term is added, so the picks step through the cycle unevenly.
steps: The picks move 3 places each time through a cycle of 4. Since $\gcd(3,4)=1$, they land on all 4 spots before repeating: $t_3, t_2, t_1, t_4$, then again.
So every 4 picks add up to one whole cycle: $2+\frac13-\frac12-3=-\frac76$.
$t_3$ to $t_{60}$ is $\frac{60}{3}=20$ picks, which is $\frac{20}{4}=5$ full rounds: $5\times(-\frac76)=\mathbf{-\tfrac{35}{6}}$.
If the gcd were bigger (step 2 through a cycle of 4), the picks would land on only $\frac42=2$ of the spots, and a round would be just those.

cards.name: Repeating decimal with a late start
cards.q: What is the sum of the 100th, 101st and 102nd digits after the decimal point of $\frac{5}{28}$?
cards.spot: a far-off digit of a fraction whose denominator has a 2 or 5 in it, so some digits come before the loop.
steps: Divide carefully: $\frac{5}{28}=0.17857142857\ldots=0.17\overline{857142}$. The **17** never repeats (2 digits); the block **857142** is 6 long.
Skip the 2 lead-in digits: the 100th digit is the $100-2=98$th digit of the block.
$98=(6\times16)+\mathbf{2}$, so the 100th, 101st and 102nd digits are the block's 2nd, 3rd and 4th: 5, 7 and 1.

cards.name: $k$ in the denominator: split and cancel
cards.q: What is $\frac{1}{1\cdot2}+\frac{1}{2\cdot3}+\frac{1}{3\cdot4}+\cdots+\frac{1}{99\cdot100}$?
cards.spot: each term is $\frac{1}{k(k+1)}$ or similar: $k$ is in the formula, so nothing loops.
steps: Split each term: $\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=\frac1k-\frac{1}{k+1}$.
Write it out: $(1-\frac12)+(\frac12-\frac13)+\cdots+(\frac{1}{99}-\frac{1}{100})$. Every middle piece cancels with its neighbour.
Only the first and last survive: $1-\frac{1}{100}=\mathbf{\tfrac{99}{100}}$.

cards.variant: even/odd parity of sums and products of unknown integers
cards.name: Count or size?
cards.text: "the greatest **number of** the integers" / "how many" asks for a **count**; "the greatest value" / "the largest integer" asks for a **size**
cards.note: odd sum: the odds come in an odd count; even product: at least one is even
cards.example: 7 integers, odd sum, even product: at most $6$ odd, and the count must be odd, so **5** are odd (not a value like $99$)

cards.text: An inequality works like an equation with **one extra rule**: multiply or divide by a negative and you must flip the sign.

cards.q: How many integers $x$ make $|x-1|+|x-5|\le6$ true?
steps: $|x-1|$ is the distance from $x$ to 1, so this says: distance to 1 + distance to 5 is at most 6.
Anywhere between 1 and 5 the total is 4. Each step outside adds 2.
So you can go 1 step past each end: $0\le x\le6$.

cards.name: $(x-a)(x-b)$, $a<b$
cards.text: $<0$ **between** $a$ and $b$; $>0$ **outside**

cards.name: $|x-a|$
cards.text: how far $x$ is from $a$

cards.name: Two lines, same slope
cards.text: **no solution**; same line: **infinitely many**

cards.name: Two inequalities
cards.text: solve each, draw both, keep the overlap

cards.name: $k^2=36$
cards.text: try **both** $6$ and $-6$ in the question

cards.name: Backsolve
cards.text: plug answer choices in, starting from the middle value
cards.note: too big? go smaller; it halves the work

cards.name: Asked for $x+y$
cards.text: add or subtract whole equations

cards.name: Difference of squares
cards.note: also products either side of a round number

cards.name: Given $a+b$ and $ab$
cards.note: with root sums: $\frac1p+\frac1q=\frac{p+q}{pq}$

cards.name: Open or closed endpoint
cards.text: $<$ leaves the endpoint out; $\le$ keeps it

cards.name: "No solution"
cards.text: same slope, **different** line
cards.note: not the value that makes them identical

patterns.title: Two swimmers, second meeting
patterns.idea: Two swimmers start at the same moment from opposite ends of a $50$ m pool and turn at each wall. The **first** meeting is always head-on, at $t=\frac{50}{v_f+v_s}$. For the **second** meeting, divide the faster speed by the slower one **before anything else**. Under 2: they cross head-on again, after covering $150$ m between them. Exactly 2: they arrive at the same wall together. Over 2: the fast swimmer turns and catches the slow one from behind, once it is $50$ m further along than the slow one.

patterns.title: Percent of which base?
patterns.idea: Before you multiply, find the noun right after **"percent of"** (or after **"than"**): that is the base. It may be a value you don't know yet (the new price, the new total). Then the percent sits on **both sides** of the equation, and you solve for the base instead of multiplying by it.

cards.text: Find the thing that **doesn't change** and build your equation around it.

cards.q: A club's ratio of boys to girls is $2:3$. After 10 boys join, the ratio is $1:1$. How many people were in the club before?
steps: The girls don't change. Call them $3k$; the boys were $2k$.
After: boys $2k+10$ = girls $3k$, so $k=10$.
Before: $2k+3k=5k=$ **50** people. (They asked for 'before', not after.)

cards.name: Ratio $a:b$
cards.text: amounts $ak$ and $bk$; the total is a multiple of $a+b$
cards.example: boys:girls $3:5$, so the class size is a multiple of 8; 30 is impossible

cards.name: Joining two ratios
cards.text: make the shared item match

cards.name: Same percent every period
cards.text: **multiply** by the same factor each time

cards.name: Working together
cards.note: add the rates, not the times

cards.name: Average speed, same distance each way
cards.note: total distance ÷ total time; always below $\frac{a+b}2$

cards.name: Setting up a story
cards.text: let $x$ = the smallest amount, write the rest from it
cards.example: A has 3 more than twice B: $B=x$, $A=2x+3$

cards.name: Answer what was asked
cards.text: reread the last sentence before you pick
cards.note: a middle value ($x$, one share, a rate) is often a wrong choice

cards.name: Plug back in
cards.text: test your answer in the original story, not your equation
cards.note: catches setup mistakes the algebra can't

cards.name: "When I was your age"
cards.text: four ages, **3** equal gaps
cards.note: the age gap never changes; split first-to-last into 3
cards.example: Ben was 6, Ana will be 33: gap $9$, Ben $15$, Ana $24$

cards.name: Middle step as an answer
cards.text: $x$ or one person's share is often a decoy choice
cards.example: found the younger, $x=12$; asked for the older, $2x+3=27$

cards.name: Splitting growth
cards.text: up 700% over 3 periods is $\times2$ each, not $+233\%$

cards.name: "When I was your age" gaps
cards.text: **3** equal gaps from first to last age, not 2

cards.name: Ratio under 2: second head-on crossing
cards.q: A swims at $1.25$ m/s from the 0 m wall, B at $1$ m/s from the 50 m wall. When do they meet for the second time?
cards.spot: $\frac{v_f}{v_s}<2$: both swimmers turn before they meet again.
steps: Ratio $1.25<2$, so they meet head-on, with $150$ m covered between them (one length to the first meeting, two more to the second).
$t=\frac{150}{1.25+1}=\frac{150}{2.25}=\mathbf{66.67}$ **s**. Check: A has swum $83.3$ m and B $66.7$ m, so both are at the $16.7$ m mark.

cards.name: Ratio exactly 2: tie at the wall
cards.q: A swims at $2$ m/s from the 0 m wall, B at $1$ m/s from the 50 m wall. When and where do they meet for the second time?
cards.spot: $\frac{v_f}{v_s}=2$: both formulas give the same time.
steps: First meeting: $t=\frac{50}{3}=16.67$ s, at the $33.3$ m mark.
Second: $t=\frac{50}{v_s}=\mathbf{50}$ **s**. A has swum $100$ m (there and back) and B $50$ m (one length), so both reach the **0 m wall** at the same instant.
$\frac{150}{2+1}=50$ and $\frac{50}{2-1}=50$: the two rules agree.

cards.name: Ratio over 2: overtake from behind
cards.q: A swims at $3$ m/s from the 0 m wall, B at $1$ m/s from the 50 m wall. When and where do they meet for the second time?
cards.spot: $\frac{v_f}{v_s}>2$: the fast swimmer turns and laps the slow one before the slow one reaches a wall.
steps: First meeting: $t=\frac{50}{4}=12.5$ s, at the $37.5$ m mark.
A turns at the 50 m wall at $t=16.67$ s. B is still heading for 0 m, at the $33.3$ m mark.
A catches B once A has swum $50$ m more than B: $t=\frac{50}{3-1}=\mathbf{25}$ **s**. A has swum $75$ m and B $25$ m, so they meet at the **25 m mark**.

cards.variant: profit as a percent of cost vs of price
cards.name: Profit as a percent of the new price
cards.q: A shop buys a lamp for 60 dollars and sells it for 84 dollars. If the shop had instead set the price so that its profit was $40\%$ of the selling price, with the cost unchanged, how much more would it have charged?
cards.spot: "of the selling price" means the price being set, which is unknown, so the base is the answer.
steps: Let $P$ be the new price. Profit $=0.4P$, and price $=$ cost $+$ profit: $P=60+0.4P$.
$100-84=$ **16 dollars** more. Not $0.4\times84$: the $40\%$ is of the new price, not the old one.

cards.variant: profit as a percent of cost vs of price
cards.name: Profit as a percent of the original price
cards.q: A shop buys a lamp for 60 dollars and sells it for 84 dollars. If the shop had instead set the price so that its profit was $40\%$ of the **original** selling price, with the cost unchanged, how much more would it have charged?
cards.spot: "original" pins the base to a number you already have: 84 dollars. Nothing to solve for.
steps: Profit $=0.4\times84=33.60$.
$93.60-84=$ **9.60 dollars** more. One word moved the answer from 16 dollars to 9.60 dollars; both are likely choices.

cards.variant: percent comparisons in QC with unknown bases
cards.name: "More than" flipped to "less than"
cards.q: $A$ is $25\%$ more than $B$. $B$ is what percent less than $A$?
cards.spot: "more than $B$" divides by $B$; "less than $A$" divides by $A$. Same gap, different base.
steps: Pick $B=100$, so $A=125$. The gap is $25$.

cards.variant: successive percent changes and reversal (up x%, then down x%)
cards.name: A further discount off the reduced price
cards.q: A 50-dollar jacket is marked $20\%$ off, and a coupon takes a further $10\%$ off the reduced price. What does it cost?
cards.spot: "off the reduced price": the second percent is of the new price, so the discounts multiply instead of adding.
steps: $50\times0.8=40$, then $40\times0.9=$ **36 dollars** ($28\%$ off in all, not $30\%$).
Had the coupon said "$10\%$ of the original price", it would take 5 dollars: $40-5=35$.

cards.variant: mixing two solutions to a target concentration
cards.name: A percent of the new mixture
cards.q: How many liters of water must be added to $20$ L of a $15\%$ salt solution so that salt is $10\%$ of the new solution?
cards.spot: "of the new solution": the base grows with the water you add, so the unknown is in the base.
steps: Salt doesn't change: $0.15\times20=3$ L.
$3=0.10(20+w)$, so $20+w=30$ and $w=$ **$10$ L**. Check: $3$ L of salt in $30$ L is $10\%$. Setting $3=0.10\times20$ leaves no room for the water.

cards.variant: finding the original value after a change
cards.name: Back out the price before a change
cards.q: After a $20\%$ increase, a ticket costs 60 dollars. What did it cost before?
cards.spot: The $20\%$ is of the old price, which is the unknown, not of the 60 dollars you are given.
steps: Not $60-0.2\times60=48$: that takes $20\%$ of the new price. Check: $50\times1.2=60$.

patterns.title: Probability density: probability is area
patterns.idea: For a density curve, **probability is area under the curve, never its height**, and the whole area is $1$. GRE densities are made of rectangles and straight lines, so every question turns into width $\times$ height or $\frac12\times$ base $\times$ height. **Sketch it first**, mark the region they ask about, then measure it.

patterns.title: Quartiles and IQR: split in half, or jump to the position
patterns.idea: Sort the list first. **Q1 is the median of the lower half and Q3 the median of the upper half**; the IQR is $Q_3-Q_1$. That is the GRE's rule. With an odd count, the median belongs to **neither** half. For a long list or a frequency table, skip the splitting and go straight to the position.

cards.text: When you combine groups, **group size matters**: a big group pulls the average toward itself.

cards.q: Class A has 10 students averaging 80. Class B has 30 students averaging 60. What is the average of all 40?
steps: Totals: $10\times80=800$ and $30\times60=1800$.
Not 70! The bigger class pulls the average toward 60.

cards.name: z-score
cards.note: compare values from two bell curves by their z-scores

cards.name: What moves the SD
cards.text: add $c$: same · multiply by $k$: $\times|k|$ · add a value at the mean: **smaller**

cards.name: Adding values and the IQR
cards.text: new max/min only: IQR stays · values on top: IQR can go **either way** · one below, one above: IQR **can't shrink**
cards.note: unknown list? try one with ties and one with a gap

cards.name: Weighted average
cards.text: group sizes = distances to the combined mean, **swapped**
cards.note: the mean sits closer to the bigger group

cards.name: Two groups, different SDs
cards.text: measure the cutoff in each group's **own** SDs
cards.example: cutoff 80: A (mean 70, SD 5) is $+2$ SD, B (mean 60, SD 20) $+1$ SD, so more of B is above

cards.name: Reading a chart
cards.text: check units and scale (thousands? percent?) before any math
cards.note: estimate first; choices are often far apart

cards.name: Density questions
cards.text: sketch, shade, cut into rectangles and triangles
cards.note: a middle slice: $1-$ the tails

cards.name: Beyond 1 SD
cards.text: $32\%$ is **both** tails; one side is $16\%$

cards.name: Extreme values and quartiles
cards.text: adding them **does** move Q1 and Q3
cards.note: they change how many values are in each half

cards.name: Median of a lopsided density
cards.text: not the middle of the range: it leans to the **tall** side
cards.note: half the **area** on each side, not half the width

cards.name: Bell curve
cards.text: use 68–95 and symmetry
cards.note: its areas can't be measured with shapes

cards.name: Table of values
cards.text: add the listed probabilities
cards.note: a discrete variable has no area

cards.name: Textbook interpolation
cards.text: not the GRE's rule
cards.note: $\frac{n+1}{4}$ for every $n$ with a split gap (position 2.75): for even $n$ use $\frac{n+2}{4}$, so 10 numbers give $Q_1=x_3$

cards.name: Boxplot given
cards.text: read Q1 and Q3 off the box edges

cards.name: Uniform: a flat rectangle
cards.q: $X$ is uniformly distributed on $2\le x\le6$. What is $P(X>5)$?
cards.spot: 'uniformly distributed on' an interval, or 'the density is a constant $c$' on it and $0$ outside.
steps: Width $6-2=4$. Area must be $1$, so the height is $\frac14$: the top line is $y=\frac14$.
$X>5$ is the strip from $5$ to $6$: width $1$, height $\frac14$.
$P=1\times\frac14=\mathbf{\frac14}$. Shortcut: probability = (slice width) $\div$ (total width) $=\frac14$.

cards.name: Triangle: one corner
cards.q: The density of $X$ rises in a straight line from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$, then falls to $(2,0)$. What is $P(X>\frac32)$?
cards.spot: a density drawn or described as straight lines, and the question asks about one end.
steps: Line for $1\le x\le2$: through $(1,1)$ and $(2,0)$, slope $-1$, so $y=2-x$.
The region right of $\frac32$ is a right triangle: base $2-\frac32=\frac12$, height $2-\frac32=\frac12$.
Area $=\frac12\times\frac12\times\frac12=\mathbf{\frac18}$.
Shortcut: the corner is a smaller copy of the right half (area $\frac12$) with half its base, so $\left(\frac12\right)^2\times\frac12=\frac18$.

steps: Check the total: rectangle $2\times\frac13=\frac23$, plus triangle $\frac12\times2\times\frac13=\frac13$. Total $1$.
The falling line goes from $(2,\frac13)$ to $(4,0)$, so at $x=3$ the height is $\frac16$.
Right of $3$: $\frac12\times1\times\frac16=\mathbf{\frac1{12}}$. Or by the corner shortcut: $\left(\frac12\right)^2\times\frac13=\frac1{12}$.

cards.name: Even count: cut into two halves
cards.spot: a short sorted list (or one you can sort) with an even count.
steps: 10 numbers: halves of 5. Lower half $3,4,\mathbf{6},7,9$, upper half $10,12,\mathbf{15},16,20$.
$Q_1$ = middle of the lower half $=6$. $Q_3$ = middle of the upper half $=15$.
IQR $=15-6=\mathbf{9}$.
If a half has an even count (12 numbers give halves of 6), its median is the average of its two middle numbers: $Q_1=\frac{x_3+x_4}{2}$, $Q_3=\frac{x_9+x_{10}}{2}$.

cards.name: Odd count: leave the median out
cards.spot: an odd count, so one number sits exactly in the middle.
steps: 7 numbers: the median is the 4th, $8$. Set it aside.
Lower half $3,\mathbf{5},6$, so $Q_1=5$. Upper half $10,\mathbf{11},15$, so $Q_3=11$.
IQR $=11-5=\mathbf{6}$. (Putting the 8 into both halves would give $Q_1=5.5$ and $Q_3=10.5$: wrong.)

cards.name: Long list: jump to the position
cards.q: 30 scores: four 1s, six 2s, nine 3s, seven 4s and four 5s. What is the IQR?
cards.spot: a frequency table, or a list too long to write out ('40 test scores').
steps: Median position: $\frac{n+1}{2}$. Q1 position: $\frac{n+1}{4}$ if $n$ is **odd**, $\frac{n+2}{4}$ if $n$ is **even**. Q3 is the mirror image: position $(n+1)-$ Q1's position.
$n=30$ is even: $Q_1$ is the $\frac{32}{4}=8$th value and $Q_3$ the $31-8=23$rd.
Running totals: the 1s fill positions 1–4, the 2s 5–10, the 3s 11–19, the 4s 20–26, the 5s 27–30.
8th value $=2$, 23rd value $=4$. IQR $=4-2=\mathbf{2}$.
A position ending in .5 (like 3.5) means the average of the two values around it ($x_3$ and $x_4$). With this rule a position is always a whole number or a .5.

cards.name: Values added at one end: the IQR can go either way
cards.q: $x_1\le x_2\le\dots\le x_{10}$ are 10 weights. Two more weights, both heavier than $x_{10}$, are added. Quantity A: the IQR of all 12. Quantity B: the IQR of the first 10.
cards.spot: a QC that adds or removes values when the actual list isn't given.
steps: First 10: halves of 5, so $Q_1=x_3$ and $Q_3=x_8$. IQR $=x_8-x_3$.
All 12: halves of 6, so $Q_1=\frac{x_3+x_4}{2}$ and $Q_3=\frac{x_9+x_{10}}{2}$. Both quartiles stay or move up; the question is which moves more.
Q3 climbs more: $1,2,\dots,10$, then add $11,12$. IQR goes from $8-3=5$ to $9.5-3.5=6$ (bigger).
Ties, so nothing moves: $1,2,3,3,5,6,7,9,9,9$, then add $10,11$. $Q_1$ stays $3$, $Q_3$ stays $9$, IQR $6$ both times (same).
Q1 climbs more (a big gap from $x_3$ to $x_4$, with $x_8,x_9,x_{10}$ bunched): $1,2,3,9,10,11,12,13,13,13$, then add $14,15$. IQR goes from $13-3=10$ to $13-6=7$ (smaller).
All three can happen, so the answer is **(D)**. Evenly spaced lists are a trap here: they always make the IQR grow.

patterns.title: Repeating decimal to fraction
patterns.idea: Call the decimal $x$. Multiply by $10$ once for each repeating digit (so by 10, 100 or 1,000), then subtract $x$. The endless tail cancels, leaving the repeating block over that many 9s.

patterns.title: FROZEN: which numbers to test
patterns.idea: When a comparison has variables, write **F R O Z E N** at the top of your scratch paper and cross off each kind as you test it: **F**ractions ($\frac12$, $-\frac12$), **R**epeats (the same number for two letters, unless told they're different), **O**ne ($1$ and $-1$), **Z**ero, **E**xtremes ($100$, $-100$), **N**egatives ($-2$, $-3$). Skip the ones the condition rules out. Two different winners means **(D)**.

cards.text: In comparison questions, try to **break** the comparison. If two different numbers give different winners, the answer is (D).

cards.q: $-1<x<1$. Compare A: $x^2$ and B: $x$.
steps: Try $x=\frac12$: A $=\frac14$, B $=\frac12$. B wins.
Try $x=-\frac12$: A $=\frac14$, B $=-\frac12$. A wins.
Different winners, so the answer is **(D)**.

cards.name: Between 0 and 1
cards.text: squaring makes it **smaller**; $\frac1x>1$

cards.name: Four zones
cards.note: find the zone first; check with $2$, $\frac12$, $-\frac12$, $-2$

cards.name: $0.\overline{9}$
cards.text: **exactly** $1$

cards.name: Repeating decimal
cards.text: the block over that many 9s

cards.name: Zero: a factor you cancelled
cards.q: $a^2b=4b$ and $ab=2b$. Compare A: $a$ and B: $2$.
cards.spot: both equations share the factor $b$, and dividing by it assumes $b\ne0$.
steps: If $b\ne0$: $a^2=4$ and $a=2$ agree, so $a=2$. Equal.
If $b=0$: both equations read $0=0$ for **every** $a$. Try $a=-7$: B is bigger.
Two different results, so **(D)**. Factor instead of dividing: $b(a^2-4)=0$ means $b=0$ **or** $a^2=4$.
cards.variant: sign cases: negatives, zero and fractions between 0 and 1

cards.name: Zero: allowed by the condition
cards.q: $|x|=-x$. Compare A: $x$ and B: $0$.
cards.spot: $|x|=-x$ reads as "$x$ is negative", but $|0|=-0$ works too.
steps: $|x|=-x$ holds for every $x\le0$, zero included.
$x=-3$: B is bigger. $x=0$: equal.
So **(D)**, not (B).
cards.variant: sign cases: negatives, zero and fractions between 0 and 1

cards.name: Fractions: a rounding condition
cards.q: $x$ rounded to the nearest integer is $3$. Compare A: $x^2$ rounded to the nearest integer, and B: $9$.
cards.spot: the condition names an integer, but $x$ itself doesn't have to be one.
steps: $x=3$: $9$ rounds to $9$. Equal.
$x=3.4$: $11.56$ rounds to $12$. A is bigger.
Two different results, so **(D)**. Testing only $x=3$ gives (C).
cards.variant: non-integer test values that flip the relationship

cards.name: Repeats: two letters, same number
cards.q: $x$ and $y$ are positive integers, and $x+y=6$. Compare A: $xy$ and B: $9$.
cards.spot: nothing says $x\ne y$, so try $x=y$.
steps: $x=1$, $y=5$: $xy=5$, B is bigger. $x=2$, $y=4$: $8$, still B.
$x=y=3$: $xy=9$. Equal.
So **(D)**. Trying only different pairs gives (B).

cards.name: One: where powers stop growing
cards.q: $n$ is a positive integer. Compare A: $n^n$ and B: $n!$.
cards.spot: "positive integer" starts at $1$, where every power and every factorial is $1$.
steps: $n=2$: $4$ against $2$. A is bigger, and it stays bigger for every larger $n$.
So **(D)**. Starting at $n=2$ gives (A).

cards.name: Extremes: both ends of a range
cards.q: $0<x<1$. Compare A: $\frac1x$ and B: $x+1.5$.
cards.spot: a range means testing **near both ends**, not just its friendly middle.
steps: $x=\frac12$: $2$ against $2$. Equal, which tempts (C).
$x=0.01$: $100$ against $1.51$. A is bigger.
$x=0.99$: about $1.01$ against $2.49$. B is bigger. So **(D)**.
cards.variant: both quantities depend on one variable with a restricted range

cards.name: Negatives: a second zone
cards.q: $x^3>x$. Compare A: $x^2$ and B: $-x$.
cards.spot: $x^3>x$ looks like "$x>1$", but a negative zone hides in it.
steps: Factor: $x(x-1)(x+1)>0$ holds for $x>1$ **and** for $-1<x<0$.
$x=2$: $4$ against $-2$. A is bigger.
$x=-\frac12$: $\frac14$ against $\frac12$. B is bigger. So **(D)**.
cards.variant: sign cases: negatives, zero and fractions between 0 and 1

cards.text: $x^2=16$ allows $\pm4$; $\sqrt{16}$ is only $4$
cards.note: whole number? positive, or just nonzero?

cards.text: divide out (if positive) or subtract it from both

cards.note: watch for "different" or "whole" numbers

cards.text: a bigger percent isn't a bigger amount: usually (D)

cards.name: 1 repeating digit
cards.q: Write $0.\overline{7}$ as a fraction.
cards.spot: one digit repeats, so multiply by $10$.
steps: $10x=7.\overline{7}$ and $x=0.\overline{7}$.
$10x-x=9x=7$, so $x=\mathbf{\frac79}$.

cards.name: 2 repeating digits
cards.q: Write $0.\overline{36}$ as a fraction.
cards.spot: two digits repeat, so multiply by $100$.
steps: $100x=36.\overline{36}$ and $x=0.\overline{36}$.

cards.name: 3 repeating digits
cards.q: Write $0.\overline{123}$ as a fraction.
cards.spot: three digits repeat, so multiply by $1{,}000$.
steps: $1000x=123.\overline{123}$ and $x=0.\overline{123}$.
